rationale: Highly anticholinergic; clearance reduced with advanced age. Risk of confusion, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and other anticholinergic effects. Tolerance develops when used as hypnotics. Diphenhydramine use increases risk of dementia.
exceptions: Diphenhydramine may be acceptable in acute treatment of severe allergic reactions when alternatives are unavailable.

rationale: Highly anticholinergic and sedating. Risk of EPS, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and respiratory depression. Multiple safer alternatives available for nausea and allergic conditions.
exceptions: None

rationale: Not recommended for prevention of extrapyramidal symptoms with antipsychotics. More effective agents available for treatment of Parkinson disease. High anticholinergic burden contributes to cognitive impairment, delirium, falls.
exceptions: May be acceptable for acute dystonic reactions when no alternative is available.

rationale: Highly anticholinergic, uncertain effectiveness at doses tolerated by older adults. Risk of cognitive impairment, constipation, urinary retention, and delirium.
exceptions: Short-term use for acute GI spasm when non-anticholinergic agents have failed.

rationale: Anticholinergic adverse effects including cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, constipation, and dry mouth. Oral immediate-release oxybutynin has highest CNS penetration and risk. Limited effectiveness for urge urinary incontinence in older adults.
exceptions: Extended-release formulations of tolterodine or trospium (less CNS penetration) may be reasonable if nonpharmacologic approaches and mirabegron have failed.

rationale: Older adults have increased sensitivity to benzodiazepines and decreased metabolism of long-acting agents. All benzodiazepines increase risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle crashes in older adults.
exceptions: Seizure disorders, benzodiazepine withdrawal, severe generalized anxiety disorder, periprocedural anesthesia, end-of-life care.

rationale: Long half-life in older adults (diazepam half-life up to 200 hours in elderly); produces prolonged sedation, increased risk of falls and fractures. Active metabolites accumulate. Higher risk of cognitive impairment than shorter-acting agents.
exceptions: Seizure disorders, benzodiazepine withdrawal, ethanol withdrawal, end-of-life care.

rationale: Benzodiazepine receptor agonists have adverse events similar to benzodiazepines in older adults including delirium, falls, fractures, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and motor vehicle crashes. Minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration. Zolpidem ER should especially be avoided.
exceptions: None

rationale: Increased risk of cerebrovascular accident (stroke), greater rate of cognitive decline, and mortality in persons with dementia. Avoid use for behavioral problems of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacological options have failed or are not possible and the older adult poses a substantial threat to self or others.
exceptions: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, short-term use as antiemetic during chemotherapy, Parkinson disease psychosis (pimavanserin preferred).

rationale: High rate of physical dependence, tolerance to sleep benefits, greater risk of overdose at low dosages compared to benzodiazepines. Risk of respiratory depression, cognitive impairment, falls.
exceptions: Seizure disorders (phenobarbital only when newer antiepileptics have failed).

rationale: Lack of efficacy. No proven benefit for dementia or any other condition in older adults.
exceptions: None

rationale: Highly anticholinergic, sedating, and cause orthostatic hypotension. Doxepin >6 mg/day has strong anticholinergic and sedative properties. Risk of falls, fractures, cognitive impairment, and cardiac conduction disturbances in older adults.
exceptions: Doxepin at doses ≤6 mg/day for insomnia may be acceptable.

rationale: Dual orexin receptor antagonists may cause next-day impairment, risk of falls, and CNS depression. Limited data in adults ≥75 years. Lower doses should be used.
exceptions: May use at lowest effective dose when nonpharmacological sleep interventions have failed.

rationale: High risk of orthostatic hypotension, especially in older adults. Associated with syncope, falls, and fractures. Should not be used as routine treatment for hypertension due to poor cardiovascular outcomes compared to other antihypertensives.
exceptions: Acceptable for BPH when other agents are not appropriate. Prazosin acceptable for PTSD-related nightmares.

rationale: High risk of CNS adverse effects including sedation, bradycardia, and orthostatic hypotension. Clonidine carries rebound hypertension risk if abruptly discontinued. Methyldopa may cause bradycardia and exacerbate depression. Not recommended as routine first-line antihypertensive.
exceptions: Clonidine may be used for cancer pain or as adjunct in ADHD. Methyldopa is acceptable during pregnancy (not applicable to ≥65 population).

drug_class: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker - immediate release
rationale: Immediate-release nifedipine causes reflex tachycardia and hypotension. Associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction and mortality. Risk of precipitous and unpredictable blood pressure drops.
exceptions: Extended-release nifedipine is acceptable and not included in this recommendation.

rationale: Decreased renal clearance of digoxin in older adults may lead to increased risk of toxicity. Doses >0.125 mg/day are associated with no additional benefit and increased risk of toxicity including nausea, vomiting, arrhythmias, and visual disturbances. Narrow therapeutic index.
exceptions: Doses ≤0.125 mg/day may be appropriate for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or rate control in atrial fibrillation when other agents have failed. Target serum level 0.5-0.9 ng/mL.

rationale: Amiodarone is associated with multiple toxicities including thyroid disease (both hypo- and hyperthyroidism), pulmonary toxicity (potentially fatal), hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuropathy, and QT prolongation. Effective for maintaining sinus rhythm but toxicity risk is high in older adults.
exceptions: May be used as first-line therapy for rate control or rhythm control in atrial fibrillation when other agents have failed or are contraindicated, particularly in structural heart disease.

rationale: Disopyramide is a potent negative inotrope and may cause heart failure and has strong anticholinergic effects. Data on other antiarrhythmics limited in adults >65. Rate control generally preferred over rhythm control for most older adults with atrial fibrillation.
exceptions: May be used when supervised by a cardiologist for specific arrhythmias when benefits outweigh risks.

rationale: Short-acting dipyridamole (oral immediate-release) may cause orthostatic hypotension. More effective alternatives exist. Should not be used as monotherapy for secondary stroke prevention.
exceptions: Extended-release dipyridamole combined with aspirin (Aggrenox) is acceptable for secondary stroke prevention.

rationale: Safer and more effective alternatives available (clopidogrel, ticagrelor). Ticlopidine has been associated with neutropenia, agranulocytosis, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and aplastic anemia.
exceptions: None

rationale: Glyburide has prolonged half-life in older adults and higher risk of severe prolonged hypoglycemia compared to other sulfonylureas. Chlorpropamide has prolonged half-life, can cause SIADH and prolonged hypoglycemia. Risk is compounded by irregular meal patterns and renal impairment common in elderly.
exceptions: Shorter-acting sulfonylureas (glipizide, glimepiride at low doses) may be acceptable with careful monitoring.

rationale: Minimal effect on weight gain in older adults. Increases risk of thrombotic events, fluid retention, and possibly death. Not an effective appetite stimulant in older adults despite common use for this indication.
exceptions: Palliative care for cancer-related cachexia when benefits outweigh risks.

rationale: Concerns about cardiac effects due to variable T3 content. Supraphysiologic T3 levels may cause cardiac arrhythmias, angina, and osteoporosis. Standardized synthetic levothyroxine preferred.
exceptions: None; levothyroxine is the standard of care.

rationale: Effect on body composition is small and associated with edema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome, gynecomastia, impaired fasting glucose. Except for established growth hormone deficiency, risk outweighs benefit in older adults.
exceptions: Documented growth hormone deficiency confirmed by appropriate testing.

rationale: Potential for cardiac problems including MI and stroke. Methyltestosterone specifically associated with hepatotoxicity. Should not be used for age-related low testosterone without clinical hypogonadism. Risk of polycythemia, prostate issues.
exceptions: Confirmed symptomatic hypogonadism with documented low testosterone levels.

rationale: Evidence of carcinogenic potential (breast and endometrial cancer) and lack of cardioprotective effect in older women. Oral and patch forms increase risk of thromboembolism and stroke.
exceptions: Topical vaginal low-dose estrogen for urogenital atrophy is acceptable.

rationale: Sliding scale insulin alone (without basal insulin) leads to higher risk of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia without improvement in glycemic management in older adults. Should be used as part of a comprehensive insulin regimen, not as sole therapy.
exceptions: Use as correction dose insulin is acceptable when combined with a basal insulin regimen.

rationale: Can cause extrapyramidal effects including tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. Risk increases with duration of use and in older adults. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome has been reported. Risk of parkinsonism.
exceptions: Acceptable for gastroparesis if no alternative is available; limit use to ≤12 weeks unless benefit clearly outweighs risk.

rationale: Oral mineral oil has potential for aspiration and aspiration pneumonia, especially in older adults with swallowing difficulties or when taken in supine position. Interferes with absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.
exceptions: None

rationale: Long-term PPI use (>8 weeks) in older adults is associated with increased risk of C. difficile infection, bone loss, fractures (hip, wrist, spine), hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, acute interstitial nephritis, CKD progression, community-acquired pneumonia, and fundic gland polyps.
exceptions: Appropriate for high-risk patients (e.g., Barrett esophagus, erosive esophagitis, pathological hypersecretory conditions, concurrent chronic NSAID use with bleeding risk). Reassess and step down therapy when possible.

rationale: Increased risk of GI bleeding/peptic ulcer disease, acute kidney injury, fluid retention, and exacerbation of heart failure. Risk increases with longer duration and higher dose. Risk is substantially higher in adults ≥75 or those taking corticosteroids, anticoagulants, or antiplatelet agents.
exceptions: Short-term use (≤1 week) with gastroprotection (PPI) if no renal impairment, heart failure, or concurrent anticoagulation. Topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel) may be appropriate for localized pain.

rationale: Although lower GI bleeding risk than non-selective NSAIDs, COX-2 selective agents still carry cardiovascular risk (MI, stroke), renal toxicity, and fluid retention in older adults. Risk of GI events remains when used with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.
exceptions: Short-term celecoxib at lowest effective dose may be acceptable with gastroprotection in patients without cardiovascular disease or renal impairment.

rationale: Increased risk of GI bleeding, peptic ulceration, and renal impairment. Highest GI bleeding risk among NSAIDs. Older adults have decreased renal clearance.
exceptions: None for systemic use. Ophthalmic ketorolac is acceptable.

rationale: Highest incidence of CNS adverse effects (headache, dizziness, confusion) among NSAIDs. Also has highest GI adverse effect profile. Increased risk of acute kidney injury.
exceptions: Short-term use for acute gout flares if colchicine and corticosteroids are contraindicated.

rationale: Normeperidine (active metabolite) accumulates with renal impairment (common in elderly), causing seizures, myoclonus, delirium, and neurotoxicity. Not an effective oral analgesic at commonly used doses. Many safer alternatives available.
exceptions: None

rationale: Most skeletal muscle relaxants are poorly tolerated by older adults due to anticholinergic adverse effects, sedation, and risk of fracture. Carisoprodol is metabolized to meprobamate (a controlled substance with high abuse potential). Effectiveness at doses tolerated by older adults is questionable.
exceptions: Short-term use (≤1 week) for acute musculoskeletal spasm if sedation risk is acceptable and patient has no fall risk.

rationale: High risk of hyponatremia in older adults. Risk of water intoxication, seizures. Not recommended for treatment of nocturia or nocturnal polyuria in elderly due to fluid and electrolyte imbalance risks.
exceptions: Acceptable for central diabetes insipidus and hemophilia A/von Willebrand disease with appropriate sodium monitoring.

rationale: Potential for pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy with long-term use. Reduced efficacy when CrCl <30 mL/min due to inadequate urinary drug concentration.
exceptions: Short-term use (≤7 days) for uncomplicated UTI when CrCl ≥30 mL/min. Long-term prophylaxis only if no alternatives are available.

rationale: Risk of sedation, dizziness, ataxia, respiratory depression (especially when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants), cognitive impairment, and falls in older adults. Dose adjustment needed for renal impairment.
exceptions: Acceptable for neuropathic pain, seizure disorders, and post-herpetic neuralgia at lowest effective dose with renal dosing adjustment.

rationale: Older antiepileptics are CYP enzyme inducers/inhibitors with numerous drug interactions. Risk of ataxia, cognitive impairment, hyponatremia (carbamazepine), osteoporosis with chronic use, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Narrow therapeutic index.
exceptions: Acceptable for seizure disorders when newer agents (levetiracetam, lamotrigine) are not appropriate. Monitor levels closely.

rationale: Risk of major bleeding increases with age and outweighs cardiovascular benefit for primary prevention in adults ≥70. The ASPREE trial showed increased all-cause mortality and major hemorrhage without cardiovascular benefit in healthy older adults.
exceptions: Secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease (established CVD, prior MI, prior stroke/TIA) is appropriate.

rationale: Avoid in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to negative inotropic effects. Risk of constipation (especially verapamil), bradycardia, heart block. Avoid combination with beta-blockers.
exceptions: Acceptable for rate control in atrial fibrillation and stable angina when beta-blockers are contraindicated, in patients without HFrEF.

rationale: Concomitant use of ≥3 CNS-active drugs substantially increases the risk of falls, fractures, respiratory depression, over-sedation, delirium, and mortality in older adults. Risk is synergistic, not just additive.
exceptions: May be unavoidable in certain psychiatric conditions or end-of-life care; minimize number and dose.

rationale: Substantially increased risk of peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding. The combination has synergistic GI toxicity. Risk is magnified in older adults, especially those on anticoagulants.
exceptions: If combination cannot be avoided, use gastroprotection with PPI. Use lowest effective doses and shortest duration.

rationale: Concurrent use of opioids and benzodiazepines greatly increases the risk of respiratory depression, overdose, and death. FDA black box warning. Risk is especially high in older adults with diminished respiratory reserve.
exceptions: End-of-life/palliative care or when alternatives are not available; use lowest effective doses with close monitoring.

rationale: Concomitant use increases risk of sedation, respiratory depression, and death. Risk is dose-dependent and particularly dangerous in older adults, those with renal impairment, or those with sleep apnea.
exceptions: May be needed for multimodal pain management; if combined, use lowest effective doses and monitor closely for respiratory depression.

drug_class: ACE inhibitor/ARB + potassium-sparing diuretic + NSAID (Triple Whammy)
rationale: Triple combination ('triple whammy') of ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID significantly increases risk of acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and hospitalization. Each component reduces renal perfusion or potassium excretion; the combination is synergistically nephrotoxic.
exceptions: If all three are clinically necessary, monitor renal function and potassium closely (within 1 week of initiation and regularly thereafter). Avoid if possible.

rationale: NSAIDs increase INR and inhibit platelet function, leading to substantially increased risk of GI and other bleeding when combined with warfarin. Even short-term NSAID use with warfarin significantly elevates bleeding risk.
exceptions: If absolutely necessary, use celecoxib at lowest dose with PPI gastroprotection and closely monitor INR.

rationale: ACE inhibitors reduce lithium clearance, increasing risk of lithium toxicity (tremor, ataxia, renal impairment, arrhythmias, seizures). Older adults have decreased renal function baseline making toxicity more likely.
exceptions: If combination cannot be avoided, reduce lithium dose and monitor lithium levels closely (within 1 week of ACE inhibitor initiation and regularly).

rationale: Both ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics independently increase serum potassium. Combined use substantially increases risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia, particularly in older adults with renal impairment or diabetes.
exceptions: Spironolactone/eplerenone at low doses in HFrEF is guideline-directed therapy. Monitor potassium and renal function within 1 week and regularly.

rationale: Anticholinergic burden is cumulative. Combining multiple anticholinergic drugs dramatically increases risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, urinary retention, and constipation. Total anticholinergic burden is more predictive than individual drug effects.
exceptions: Minimize total anticholinergic burden. Substitute non-anticholinergic alternatives whenever possible.

rationale: Triple combination of anticoagulant, NSAID, and corticosteroid creates extremely high risk of GI bleeding. Each drug independently increases GI bleed risk; combination is synergistic.
exceptions: None. If anticoagulation is necessary, discontinue NSAID and/or corticosteroid. Use PPI if corticosteroid is continued.

rationale: One of the least effective antiemetics. Can cause extrapyramidal adverse effects. Many safer and more effective alternatives available.
exceptions: None

rationale: Older adults are more sensitive to opioid effects including respiratory depression, constipation, falls, nausea, and cognitive impairment. Start at 25-50% of adult dose. Avoid in patients with fall risk or cognitive impairment if possible. Codeine has unpredictable metabolism (CYP2D6). Tramadol risk of seizures, serotonin syndrome, and hypoglycemia.
exceptions: Appropriate for moderate-severe pain when non-opioid alternatives are inadequate. Use lowest effective dose, shortest duration, with bowel regimen.

rationale: Risk of lactic acidosis increases with degree of renal impairment. Should be avoided when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m² and dose-reduced when eGFR 30-45. Older adults frequently have unrecognized renal impairment.
exceptions: Safe to use at full dose when eGFR ≥45 mL/min/1.73m². Remains first-line for type 2 diabetes with adequate renal function.

rationale: Paroxetine is strongly anticholinergic and should be avoided. All SSRIs increase risk of hyponatremia (SIADH) in older adults. Risk of falls, GI bleeding (especially with anticoagulants/antiplatelets). Fluoxetine has long half-life with potential for accumulation.
exceptions: Sertraline and escitalopram preferred SSRIs in older adults due to favorable side effect profile and fewer drug interactions.

rationale: Cimetidine inhibits CYP450 enzymes leading to numerous drug interactions (warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline). Can cause mental status changes including confusion and delirium in older adults. Anti-androgenic effects. Other H2 blockers (famotidine, ranitidine alternatives) are preferred.
exceptions: None; famotidine is preferred H2 blocker when needed.

rationale: Tertiary TCAs (amitriptyline) have strong anticholinergic, sedative, and orthostatic effects. Nortriptyline and desipramine (secondary TCAs) are less anticholinergic but still carry cardiac conduction risks. Duloxetine preferred SNRI but may worsen hyponatremia.
exceptions: Duloxetine or secondary TCAs (nortriptyline, desipramine) at low doses may be acceptable for neuropathic pain when first-line agents fail.

rationale: Risk of hyperkalemia increases significantly in older adults, especially those with renal impairment, diabetes, or concurrent ACE inhibitor/ARB use. At doses >25 mg/day, risk of hyperkalemia and gynecomastia increases.
exceptions: Guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF at 12.5-25 mg/day with close monitoring of potassium and renal function.

rationale: In permanent atrial fibrillation, dronedarone doubles the risk of cardiovascular death, stroke, and heart failure hospitalization (PALLAS trial). Also carries risk of hepatotoxicity and pulmonary toxicity.
exceptions: May be used for paroxysmal/persistent AF to maintain sinus rhythm in patients without severe HF or permanent AF.
